list.listitem: Mild infection may result in only nausea, mild abdominal discomfort, mild anorexia, and/or dyspepsia, whereas more severe infection may lead to mechanical obstruction, perforation, biliary and pancreatic duct obstruction, and/or appendicitis. Many patients are asymptomatic. C
Examine a concentrated stool specimen (formalin ethyl-acetate sedimentation technique) for Ascaris eggs in a symptomatic patient, particularly if living in or returning from an endemic area. C

Abdominal ultrasound is typically the initial imaging method; however, diagnosis may require abdominal CT with oral contrast, MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) or endoscopic cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), or direct endoscopy depending on the patient's symptoms. C
First-line drug therapy is typically single-dose treatment with albendazole, mebendazole, or ivermectin, but pay attention to the age and weight limitations if prescribing for children. A

Cure is anticipated when treating isolated cases in nonendemic populations, whereas repeated treatment and prevention by improving behavioral, hygiene, and sanitation measures are crucial in endemic populations. C

background.definition: Ascariasis is an infection of the small intestine caused by the intestinal helminth, Ascaris lumbricoides, a parasitic roundworm that is the largest of the intestinal nematodes. Ascariasis is globally distributed; however, the highest frequency of infection occurs in tropical and subtropical regions and in any area with inadequate sanitation.

list.listitem: In a meta-analysis of 24 studies of helminth infection rates pre- and post-treatment, A. lumbricoides reinfection rates reached 26%, 68%, and 94% of pretreatment levels at 3, 6, and 12-months post-treatment, respectively.
Ascariasis was identified in 14 people who lived on small-scale farms and had contact with pigs in Maine during 2010 to 2013.

Approximately 772-892 million people are infected with A. lumbricoides worldwide according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Estimates from a systematic review and meta-analysis found a global prevalence rate of 11% (95% confidence interval [CI] 10.3-11.8%) using data from 616 studies representing 81 countries (2010-2021). The highest regional prevalence rate was from Oceania at 28.8% (95% CI 7.1-57.7%) and the lowest was in Eastern Asia at 1.4% (1.1-1.7%).
In a study of pregnant women in 4 provinces in Thailand, 21.6% were infected with a soil-transmitted helminth, 10.3% were A. lumbricoides .
Prevalence of A. lumbricoides among 692 children in two slum villages in Nairobi were 24.1% among preschool-age children and 22.7% among school-aged children.

In a cross-sectional population study in Panama, parasites were present in almost half of the samples from 1123 individuals, with 25.4% having a single parasite and 22.1% having more than one parasite. A. lumbricoides was an infecting parasite in 175 cases (15.6%). Risk factors for parasitic infection included belonging to an indigenous community, not wearing shoes, not having a hygienic toilet, and co-presence of commensals (microbes present on the body without causing harm)..

Among 255 Ethiopian preschool-aged children, prevalence of A. lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura, and hookworm were 10.8% (95% confidence interval [CI] 6.6-15.1), 1.4% (95% CI 0-3.0), and 0% (95% CI 0-1.7), respectively.

Ascaris eggs can be found on the hands and produce in endemic areas, making handwashing and rinsing of produce preventive strategies. In one study of 116 rural households in Kenya, Ascaris eggs were found in 0.9% of hand rinse, 3.5% of leafy produce, and 1.8% of root produce samples.
Helminth exposure/infection may reduce the immune response following tuberculosis exposure, resulting in a false negative tuberculin skin test.

In a Brazilian study, helminth infestation was present in 24% and children with high load infestation (>R = 100 eggs/g) were 5 times more likely than those with low load or no infestation to have heightened bronchial responsiveness.
Ascariasis was one of the 8 causes of chronic disease and injury affecting more than 10% of the world's population in 2015.
Transmission is via fecal-oral exposure to fertilized A. lumbrico ides eggs in soil; unfertilized eggs are not infective.
Risk of infection is highest among children in developing countries and where geophagia (earth eating) and reuse of wastewater for irrigation occurs.
Adult female worm can produce up to 200,000 eggs per day.
Eggs can remain viable in warm, moist soil for up to 6 years.
In a Chinese study, pig Ascaris was an important source of human ascariasis in endemic areas where both types exist.
Following several months of maturation, larvae form within the eggs and infective egg enters the host's jejunum.
Larvae hatch in host's jejunum and penetrate jejunal mucosa and enter the portal circulation.
The larvae then travel through the right heart into the pulmonary circulation, where they break into alveolar space and molt twice over 2-week period.
Larvae then ascend from alveoli into host's trachea and are then swallowed. Then they molt a final time in the intestine and develop into adult worm of 10 to 30 cm in length.
Adult worms can survive for 1 to 2 years.

Two loci (1 each on chromosomes 1 and 13) have been identified and are associated with significant effects on decreased susceptibility to Ascaris infection. Interestingly, some of the identified susceptibility loci found among parasitic diseases are shared with immunological disorders, suggesting that parasites may have played a role in driving the evolution of the immune system.
Education and behavior modification (ie, avoiding geophagy, proper handwashing, at least 6 months of composting human excreta before use as fertilizer). C
Ensuring safety of the water supply. C

Efficient sanitation and effective treatment of human excreta; in one meta-analysis, availability (i.e., having access at one's own household or living near a sanitation facility) and use of that facility was associated with protection against A. lumbricoides (RR 0.58; 95% CI 0.45-0.75) as well as other helminths. B
With respect to composting human waste, authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found a RR of 1.24 (95% CI 1.13-1.37) for any helminth infection with reuse of fresh excreta compared to those who do not handle excreta or who compost appropriately, although the risk for A. lumbricoides specifically did not reach statistical significance (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.87-1.58).
A school-based hygiene, water quality and sanitation intervention following school-based deworming reduced reinfection prevalence and egg count of A. lumbricoides but not of other helminth species. B
Mass deworming is effective for secondary prevention of A. lumbricoides. A

Vitamin A supplementation was not helpful in preventing reinfection among 250 Aboriginal schoolchildren in Malaysia. However, in an RCT including 343 rural primary schoolchildren in Malaysia with vitamin A deficiency who were infected with soil-transmitted helminths, 65.6% of whom had A. lumbricoides, use of red palm olein (RPO)-enriched biscuits that are high in carotenoids compared to PO-enriched biscuits following treatment with albendazole reduced reinfection rates of A. lumbricoides at 6 months (35.3% and 60%, respectively). Other helminth reinfection rates were not different by treatment group.

Nutritional supplementation for school-aged children failed to reduce re-infection rates of the three soil-transmitted helminth infections evaluated, including A. lumbricoides, based on data from 6 RCTs.

A four-monthly treatment was more effective than a single annual treatment for ascariasis (17.1% absolute difference in reduction, 95% CI 13.1-21.1%) and hookworm, based on a secondary analysis of an RCT of school-based deworming among Kenyan school children.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 38 studies of children concluded that mass deworming led to greater reduction in prevalence of A lumbricoides (OR 16.4, 95% CI 2·1-125·8) and hookworm (OR 4.6, 95% CI 1.8-11.6) compared to targeted deworming; no effect was seen for Trichuris trichiura.
Many patients are asymptomatic, and mild infection may result in only nausea, mild abdominal discomfort, mild anorexia, and/or dyspepsia. C
More severe infection may lead to mechanical obstruction, perforation, biliary and pancreatic duct obstruction, and/or appendicitis. C

Diagnosis is made by identifying A. lumbricoides eggs by microscopy in fresh or fixed stool specimens or by the passage of adult worms from the patient's nose, mouth, or anus. C Use of a single real-time PCR appears to be as sensitive as the quadruplicate Kato-Katz method for microscopic detection of eggs in stool samples. B
Most people infected with A. lumbricoides are asymptomatic.

Early infection (initial 2 weeks) may include pulmonary symptoms including nonproductive cough, fever, and chest pain and laboratory evidence of peripheral eosinophilia on CBC. These symptoms correlate with a hypersensitivity response to the phase of pulmonary infection in the Ascaris life cycle.
Eosinophilic pneumonia (Löeffler syndrome) may occur in severe cases.
Abdominal symptoms depend on the severity of infection.
Mild infection may result in only nausea, mild abdominal discomfort, mild anorexia, and/or dyspepsia.

Moderate and heavy infections may lead to mechanical obstruction of the intestine with perforation, biliary and pancreatic duct obstruction, and/or appendicitis. In a case series of 9 patients with biliary ascariasis, eight presented with acute abdominal pain radiating to the back and one patient presented with features of acute cholecystitis.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 86 studies from India of extra-intestinal ascariasis found that 78% involved the hepato-biliary-pancreatic (HBP) organs, most commonly the bile duct (53.6%). Significant associations with HBP infection included female gender (OR 11.3, 95% CI 2.8 to 44.9) and previous gallbladder disease. Ocular symptoms were only seen in children.
Children with ascariasis, particularly those in endemic areas, are more susceptible to anemia and malnutrition related to associated anorexia and malabsorption of nutrients.

In a 9-year cases series of 156 children with acute pancreatitis living in India in an endemic area, 60% of cases were due to biliary ascariasis. Of these, 25 of the 93 children underwent emergency ERCP for removal of worms.
In a Polish study of 252 children with ascariasis, a seasonal pattern (August-December) was observed.
Examination of a concentrated stool specimen using the formalin ethyl-acetate sedimentation technique is the preferred method of identification of Ascaris eggs.
Wet mount microscopic examination of feces can detect moderate to heavy Ascaris infections.

A quantitative assessment of infection can be obtained using the Kato-Katz method. In one study, the Kato-Katz method gave the best overall diagnostic performance in all measures (prevalence, fecal egg count, sensitivity) followed by the conventional ethyl-acetate and then the Midi Parasep(®) technique.

Collection of a second stool sample can increase diagnostic yield; in one study of 4,985 children in rural China, analysis of a second fecal sample led to increases in detection of A. Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura, and hookworm of 23%, 26%, and 100%, respectively.
Examination of sputum or gastric aspirate may identify larvae during the pulmonary migration phase of the life cycle.
Adult Ascaris worms may be identified through their outline by contrast material on an upper gastrointestinal series.
Ultrasonography may identify adult worms in the small intestine or the biliary tract.
CT scan of the abdomen with oral contrast may identify Ascaris worms in the lumen of the small bowel.
ERCP and MRCP may identify adult worms in the biliary tract.
Direct endoscopy may identify adult worms in the small intestine.
Endosonography may be comparable to ERCP for diagnosing the cause of extrahepatic biliary obstruction.

A multiplex PCR-bead protocol using fecal DNA samples may be an alternative diagnostic test for intestinal parasites. In a recent study, the sensitivity of real-time PCR compared with the Kato-Katz method at follow-up testing was 87.5% for A. lumbricoides.
Maintain high clinical suspicion in patients living in or returning from endemic areas, particularly patients with abdominal or pulmonary symptoms or with nutritional deficiencies.
Diagnosis is made by identifying Ascaris eggs in the stool or by the passage of adult worms from the patient's nose, mouth, or anus.

Medical treatment of adults and children is recommended, typically with albendazole (400 mg orally once), mebendazole (500 mg orally once or 100 mg orally twice daily for 3 days), or ivermectin (150-200 μg/kg orally once). A
At-risk groups in endemic areas may need repeated drug treatment. C
Treatment with one of the medications listed in Table 1 yield cure rates above 92% and egg reduction rates above 96% to 99%.

In a systematic review, cure rates for single-dose oral albendazole, mebendazole, and pyrantel pamoate for infection with A. lumbricoides were 88% (95% CI, 79-93; 557 patients), 95% (95% CI, 91-97; 309 patients), and 88% (95% CI, 79-93; 131 patients), respectively.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 30 parallel-group RCTs including 6442 participants found single-dose albendazole, mebendazole, and ivermectin similarly effective against A. lumbricoides infection, with high parasitological cure rates.

Authors of a systematic review confirmed that single dose therapy with albendazole, mebendazole, levamisole, and pyrantel pamoate were highly effective for A. lumbricoides but none were very effective against T. trichiura and only albendazole was reasonably effective against hookworm (cure rate of 79.5%).

While single-dose albendazole appears sufficient for treating Ascaris infection, two doses may be necessary for hookworm infestation, and even a 3-day regimen was insufficient to cure whipworm in one study.

Decreases in egg counts are greater when combining albendazole plus ivermectin (99.5%) rather than monotherapy with either albendazole (93%) or ivermectin (95%). This combination is also more effective for treating T. trichiura.
At-risk groups in endemic areas may need repeated and regular drug treatment.
Screening of stool and treatment of close contacts may be required to prevent reinfection within a family in nonendemic areas.

Although medical treatment and prevention of recurrence of ascariasis is the mainstay of treatment, surgery may be required to treat the complications of infection, including intestinal and/or biliary tract obstruction.
In the small case series of patients with biliary ascariasis noted above, endoscopic extraction of the worm from the biliary tree or duodenum was successfully undertaken in all patients.

Hospitalization is typically only required to manage complications of ascariasis such as intestinal or biliary tract obstruction or abscess formation, or to treat significant malnutrition and complications of vitamin deficiency.
In a systematic review of studies of children in India with extra-intestinal ascariasis, death was reported in 4 (3.8%) patients.
The prognosis of cure following treatment in nonendemic populations is excellent given cure rates above 92% and egg reduction rates above 96% to 99% associated with the commonly used medications. B

The prognosis of cure and avoidance of reinfection in endemic populations depends on the burden of disease in the population the ability to influence behavioral factors (e.g., geophagy) and the safety and efficiency of water and sanitation measures. C

Rapid reinfection among school-aged children with soil-transmitted helminth infection was shown in one study following triple-dose albendazole treatment. The prevalence at 4- and 6-months post-treatment for A. lumbricoides was 76% and 84%, respectively; this is higher than that of other helminth species. C In another RCT of multiple drug regimens, reinfection rates at 18 weeks post-treatment for all treatment arms were 34.6% for A. lumbricoides (95% CI, 27.3-42.3), 37.2 % for T. trichiura (95% CI, 28.3-46.8), and 25.0% for hookworms (95% CI, 15.5-36.6).

Unfortunately, deworming, including mass deworming, was not found to improve indicators of mortality, anemia, weight, or growth in children younger than five, school attendance or cognition in older children, or in the health of women of reproductive age based on two systematic reviews.

Most drugs used for the treatment of ascariasis are pregnancy category C, so the risks and benefits of treatment must be individually considered. If possible, avoid treatment in the first trimester of pregnancy.

Geophagy, the habit of deliberately eating earth, is not uncommon in many societies and has been demonstrated to be a significant risk factor for infection with A. lumbricoides as well as other helminths, and for reinfection following deworming among pregnant and postpartum women.

The relative risk for reinfection with A. lu mbricoides at delivery among women in Kenya engaged in geophagy compared with women who were not was 1.5 compared with 2.2 at 3 months postpartum and 2.4 at 6 months postpartum.

In a 9-year study of 986 Bolivian forager-horticulturalists experiencing natural fertility and 70% helminth prevalence, infection with A. lumbricoides was associated with earlier first births and shortened interbirth intervals; infection with hookworm was associated with delayed first pregnancy and extended interbirth intervals.

In a study of 178 women in Nigeria, helminth infestation, present in 31 women (15 with ascariasis), was associated with maternal anemia (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 12.4; 95% CI, 4.2-36.3) and low birth weight (adjusted OR 6.8; 95% CI, 2.1-21.9).
